engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Opening: Italian Game Basics
chess.body: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. White targets f7, the weakest square in Black's position. Giuoco Piano (3...Bc5) leads to rich middlegame. Learn: castle early, play d3, develop bishop to e3, then push d4 for centre control. Safe, instructive, good for learning. Magnus Carlsen played this at the top level.

wisdom.title: Letting Go of Control
wisdom.body: You can control your effort. You cannot control outcomes. The job market, the Instagram algorithm, the baby's sleep schedule — all outside your control. Epictetus: 'Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.'

book.author: Greg McKeown
book.chapter: The 90% Rule: If It's Not a Hell Yes, It's a No
book.lesson: McKeown's 90% rule for decisions: when evaluating an opportunity, give it a score from 0 to 100 on fit with your most important criteria. If it scores below 90, say no. This sounds extreme. In practice, it forces clarity: most things we say yes to are 60-70% fits — good enough, not great. The 60% fits crowd out the 90% opportunities that actually advance your most important goals. Every yes is an implicit no to everything else. The question is not 'is this a good opportunity?' but 'is this the best opportunity I have right now?'
book.key_quote: Every yes costs you a no somewhere else. Make sure the trade is worth it.
book.action: Apply the 90% rule to your next opportunity or request. Score it honestly. If it's below 90, practice saying a polite no.
crux: Almost everything is noise. Very few things are exceptionally valuable.
The undisciplined pursuit of more is how capable people stall.
Replace 'How can I do it all?' with 'What is the one thing I should do?'
If you don't prioritise your life, someone else will.
Trade-offs are unavoidable. Pretending otherwise means choosing badly by default.
Explore widely before committing narrowly. More options examined, fewer selected.
Apply extreme criteria: not 'is this good?' but 'is this the best possible use of this time?'
'No' is a complete sentence. The discomfort of refusing lasts minutes; the cost of agreeing lasts months.
Sunk cost is not a reason. Ask what you would pay to acquire this commitment today.
Buffer time by 50%. Every plan without slack fails on contact with reality.
Remove the bottleneck rather than working harder around it.
Small wins beat big launches. Progress is the most effective motivator known.
Essentialism is a discipline, not a one-time purge. The noise regrows weekly.
learnings: Saying yes to everything is a decision — usually a bad one made passively.
The cost of a commitment is every alternative you can no longer take.
Capable people get buried precisely because they are capable.
Slack is not waste. Slack is what absorbs reality.
examples: Southwest Airlines said no to meals, assigned seating, and hub routing — and stayed profitable for decades while full-service rivals collapsed.
Warren Buffett attributes most of his wealth to roughly ten decisions, having passed on thousands.
McKeown attended a client meeting hours after his daughter's birth. He got neither the client's respect nor the moment back — the book's founding regret.
adapt: Before any new build: what does this replace? If nothing, it doesn't start.
Kill features that no measurement supports. The deleted /fno and /options pages were the right call.
Buffer every deadline by 50%. A model promised Friday gets built by Wednesday.

health.body: 8,000 steps a day is associated with a large mortality reduction versus 4,000, and the curve is steepest at the low end. The gains come from moving more, not from moving harder.

father.title: Get down on the floor
father.do: Ten minutes of tummy-adjacent floor time where you are lying at her eye level, not looming above.

life_wisdom.apply: Before delivering hard feedback, run all four. Most feedback that lands badly is true and useful but fails on timing.

speaking.title: One breath, one idea
speaking.drill: Say your headline number, then breathe. Say the driver, then breathe. Practise with today's gross margin bridge.
speaking.why: Running clauses together is why people lose the thread of financial explanations.

interview_tech.q: Explain contribution margin versus gross margin and when each misleads.
interview_tech.a: Gross margin is revenue less cost of goods — it answers whether you bought and priced well. Contribution margin deducts all variable costs, including logistics, payment fees, markdown and returns — it answers whether the sale was worth making. Gross margin misleads for high-return or bulky goods; contribution misleads when 'variable' costs are actually committed in the short run, which makes closure decisions look better on paper than in cash. Use gross margin for buying decisions and contribution for range and channel decisions.

interview_tech.q: What is the cash conversion cycle for a fashion retailer, and how would you cut it 15 days?
interview_tech.a: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO. Fashion retail is inventory-heavy and near-zero DSO, so it is mostly DIO minus DPO. To cut 15 days: shorten the buying calendar and increase in-season replenishment so you commit later; push slow lines to markdown earlier rather than holding for full price; renegotiate supplier terms from 60 to 90 days in exchange for volume commitment; and consolidate SKUs — every incremental SKU carries safety stock. Quantify it: on AED 400M COGS, 15 days is roughly AED 16M of cash released.

interview_soft.q: How do you decide what to delegate?
interview_soft.a: Give a rule. Something like: delegate anything where the cost of a mistake is recoverable and the learning value is high; keep anything where your specific judgement is the reason the answer is right, and anything you would have to redo. The failure mode interviewers probe is the controller who keeps the technical work because it is comfortable and delegates only the admin — which caps the team's growth and yours.

interview_soft.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your CEO.
interview_soft.a: They are testing whether you have spine and judgement, not whether you win. Use STAR and pick a disagreement where you were partly wrong — it reads as honest. Cover: what the disagreement was, what evidence you brought, how you escalated it appropriately, what the decision was, and crucially what you did after the decision went against you. The signal they want: you argue hard privately and commit fully publicly.

cfo_field.q: Read the cash flow statement first. Always.
cfo_field.a: P&L is an opinion, cash is a fact. Open any set of accounts at the cash flow statement, compare operating cash flow to EBITDA over three years, and look at the gap. A business converting 90%+ of EBITDA to operating cash is real. One converting 50% has its profit sitting in working capital or is capitalising something it should be expensing. That one ratio finds more problems than any variance pack.
cfo_field.who: The first thing to check, every time

cfo_field.q: Scenario planning beats a single budget, and costs less than it sounds.
cfo_field.a: Three cases — base, downside, upside — with the two or three variables that actually move the outcome, not thirty. In retail that is usually like-for-like growth, gross margin, and rent renewals. The value is not the numbers; it is that the board has already discussed the downside before it arrives, so the conversation when it does is about the response rather than about whether it is happening.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on the opening: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6, develop the queen’s bishop to c5 instead of Bd7, and castle early; this saves ~0.5 pawns and avoids the cramped position that led to your loss.
Focus on early queen safety: after 1.e4 d5, avoid 2...Qxd5 → 3.Nc3 Qd8; instead play 2...Nf6, developing and preventing queen harassment. This cuts opponent’s tempo and reduces tactical threats.
Strengthen your endgame technique: practice converting a +0.5 pawn advantage into a win within 15 moves, focusing on king activity and precise pawn pushes.

lichess_summary.session_summary: **Verdict:** Your 33 % win rate shows you’re barely scraping past the baseline; the opening you most consistently lose with—**the Sicilian Defense, Najdorf Variation (B90–B99)**—is a liability that opponents exploit for early pressure. Switch to a more solid, low‑theory weapon such as the **London System (A02–A04)** to curb tactical mishaps and force opponents into unfamiliar territory. From now on, drill the first 12 moves of the London System until they’re second nature, then focus on mastering typical middlegame pawn breaks (e4/e5) and endgame king‑activity; any deviation back to the Najdorf should be eliminated immediately.
